texts.city: You own your home outright and have strong protection, but retirement and college funding compete with limited cash flow.
texts.strength: You hold $80,000 in cash that covers 7.9 months of essential expenses today.

cashflow.building: You save 24% of income but run a yearly shortfall of -$6,418.
cashflow.plain: You save a lot—$60,000 a year—but your spending and taxes exceed income. Think of your money like buckets: one bucket is taxable savings, another should be retirement and college, but right now only the taxable bucket is being filled.
cashflow.standard: Your income is $250,000 and you save $60,000 a year (24% of income), yet net cash flow is -$6,418 a year. Expenses are $116,100, taxes $66,818, and housing expenses $13,500 a year. Retirement accounts hold $0 while $50,000 a year goes to taxable accounts, and college needs of $98,838 compete for the same cash.

cushion.building: Your $80,000 cash exceeds the recommended reserve, but only $750 sits above near-term goals.
cushion.plain: You have more than the suggested emergency fund, so immediate risk is low. After setting aside a $6,000 vacation and Ethan’s $12,500 college payment, only a small extra cushion remains.
cushion.standard: Accessible cash is $80,000, covering 7.9 months of essential expenses before near-term goals. The recommended reserve is $50,625 to $60,750, and emergency reserve plus near-term goals is $69,125 to $79,250. After setting aside the $18,500 of near-term goals, months covered fall to 6.1 and only $750 sits above both reserve and those goals.

retirement.building: Projected savings and investments run out at age 73, leaving a large long-term gap.
retirement.plain: Your retirement plan depends heavily on savings because guaranteed income is limited. Social Security covers only part, so savings must stretch a long time.
retirement.standard: Planned spending left unpaid by the end of the plan is $1,448,673, with savings and investments running out at age 73. Yearly retirement spending need averages $153,672, and guaranteed income (Social Security) averages $38,336, covering 25% of that need. The remaining $115,335 a year would need to come from savings, and retirement accounts currently hold $0.

debt.building: You have no debt and your home is owned outright with $900,000 equity.
debt.plain: You carry no loans, so monthly income isn’t eaten by debt payments. That leaves flexibility to fund college or retirement, but cash flow still matters.
debt.standard: Total debt is $0 (0% of yearly income) and housing and debt payments equal 5.4% of income, well below lender strain thresholds. With no mortgage and $900,000 in home equity, borrowing remains an option, but the plan notes the thin cash cushion as the main pressure.

protection.building: Life, disability and umbrella cover are in place at recommended levels for your household.
protection.plain: You have life insurance and an umbrella policy to protect your family if you can’t work. These policies are sized to cover major risks so your children are protected.
protection.standard: Life insurance is $2,000,000, within the recommended $1,250,000 to $2,500,000 range, and umbrella liability cover is $2,000,000, meeting the recommended minimum. Long-term disability pays $12,500 a month, so income protection is strong and doesn’t compete with savings goals. The plan suggests confirming underlying home and auto cover for gaps under the umbrella.

college.building: College still needs $98,838 beyond current 529 balances, with Ethan starting in August 2026.
college.plain: You currently have $0 in 529s and will need more cash for both children’s tuition. College funding is near-term for Ethan and competes with retirement saving.
college.standard: Saved in 529 accounts is $0 and still to fund for college is $98,838 today. Ethan has $48,469 still to fund and starts August 2026, while Ava has $50,369 still to fund and starts August 2028. Because yearly cash flow is about -$6,418, college and retirement must be weighed as competing uses of cash.

investments.building: Most wealth is your $900,000 home; invested accounts are $335,000 with a stock allocation slightly above target.
investments.plain: Your investable assets are mostly outside retirement accounts and concentrated in a few ETFs. The house is valuable but not easily turned into yearly spending money.
investments.standard: Invested savings are $335,000 with 68% stocks, 12% bonds, 20% cash versus a target mix of 65% stocks, 14% bonds, 21% cash. Major holdings include VTI $162,000, SCHD $93,000, JNK $50,000, and VWO $30,000. No retirement accounts are listed, and you could contribute up to $7,500 to a traditional IRA and up to $4,400 to an HSA, both currently at $0.

score.building: Your published score is 82, in the strong band, with clear moves to improve it.
score.plain: An overall 82 means you’re in good shape, especially on liquidity, debt and protection. A few targeted changes could raise the score a few points.
score.standard: Score components: Savings and cash flow 22/30, Debt 20/20, Investments 10/15, Liquidity 15/15, Insurance 14/20. The top move is adding homeowners insurance to close a coverage gap (score 82 to 84). Reducing VTI concentration and adjusting growth allocation are other score-improving options.

assumptions.building: The plan assumes you retire at 65 and the plan runs to age 91 with prices rising 3% a year.
assumptions.plain: Several baseline assumptions shape the projection, like your retirement age and ongoing salary. These are the lens the plan uses to test outcomes.
assumptions.standard: Key assumptions include Samantha retires at 65, the plan runs until age 91, prices rise 3% a year, and Samantha’s salary of $250,000 continues until 2044. Social Security for Samantha is assumed to start in 2046, and the plan includes recurring items like a $6,000 vacation every year.

m0.title: Add homeowners insurance on primary home
m0.why: The plan recommends this to close a coverage gap and raises your score from 82 to 84.
steps: Confirm current home policy limits and exclusions.
Get a homeowners insurance quote for your primary home.
Buy the policy that fills the coverage gap indicated.
Record the new policy so the plan reflects updated cover.

quiz.q: What score improvement does adding homeowners insurance produce in the plan?
quiz.explain: The plan says adding homeowners insurance moves the published score from 82 to 84.

m1.title: Reduce VTI concentration
m1.why: The plan suggests cutting VTI concentration to improve investments and raise the score from 82 to 83.
steps: Check your current VTI holding and its share of investable accounts.
Decide how much of VTI to sell to reach the next band.
Execute the sell and reallocate proceeds across other holdings.
Update account records so the plan shows the new allocation.

quiz.q: How much of VTI does the plan say to shift to change the concentration band?
quiz.explain: The plan specifies about $58,300 toward reducing VTI concentration to reach the next band.

m2.title: Reduce growth allocation toward glide
m2.why: The plan recommends shifting allocation from 85% to 80% growth to better fit your horizon and raise the score.
steps: Review current invested mix showing 85% growth today.
Decide which assets equal about $17,100 to rebalance away from growth.
Sell or rebalance that amount into less growth-oriented holdings.
Confirm the new mix aligns with the 80% glide target.

quiz.q: What invested-book amount does the plan cite to move the mix toward the glide?
quiz.explain: The plan notes about $17,100 of the invested book would move the mix from 85% to 80% growth.
